segments.text: Anti-glycoprotein F (respiratory syncytial virus) monoclonal antibody Prevention of respiratory syncytial virus-associated illness
Abdul Akhir 1 , Arunava Dasgupta 1,2 and Sidharth Chopra 1,2
1 Division of Microbiology, CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow, India; 2 Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), Ghaziabad, India

Prevention of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, which leads to lower respiratory tract illness in infants as well as in older people, has become a global public health priority. There is a need for an effective prophylactic RSV vaccine that can protect infants from RSV infection. The only approved agent for RSV prophylaxis is palivizumab, but its use is limited to high-risk infants. For one RSV season, 5 doses of palivizu­ mab are required, which increases the cost per season and does not enable optimal use of palivizumab in low- and middleincome countries. In this context, nirsevimab (MEDI8897), a monoclonal antibody derived from human IgG1, is being developed by MedImmune (AstraZeneca) and Sanofi, and tar -gets conformational epitope in pre-F specific antigenic site ɸ of RSV. Three amino acids (M257Y/S259T/T261E [YTE]) have been engineered for nirsevimab in the conserved Fc region, which extends the half-life of the antibody, so just 1 dose will be required for an entire RSV season. Nirsevimab shows a significant increase in potency against RSV compared to palivi -zumab. Phase I and II clinical studies found that nirsevimab is well tolerated and safe for clinical use, and a single dose prevented RSV infection for a whole season. Globally, infants are at a high risk for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI). As estimated in 2015, on average, 33.1 million RSV LRTI episodes in children below 5 years of age, including 3.2 million hospitalizations and 118,000 deaths, are reported annually worldwide (1, 2). During the 2015-2016 season in the U.S., a multicenter surveillance found that among < 5-year-old children, RSV was associated with more than one-third of acute respiratory infections requiring hospitalization (3).
